title: Technical deep dive - Autoscaling & capacity planning
summary: Deep technical discussion on autoscaling strategies for Redwood deployments in VPC/on-prem and hosted modes. Covered burst policies, queueing models, reserved GPU sizing, warm vs cold starts, KV cache behavior under scale, batching tradeoffs, and quantization impact on latency. Agreed next steps: run bench of peak burst pattern, share design doc for pre-warm policy, provide pricing for reserved capacity and burst credits.
next_steps: Redwood to run 1-hour benchmark with customer peak QPS pattern and share results (Diego)
Send POC architecture doc for VPC deployment (Alice)
Provide reserved capacity pricing and burst credit options (Alice)
Schedule follow-up POC planning meeting next week (Owen to coordinate)
action_items: Diego Ramos | run 1-hour benchmark using 8-client QPS trace with 60s bursts | 2026-03-11
Alice Carter | send VPC/private deployment architecture doc + security whitepaper | 2026-03-06
Maya Patel | share historical token-per-second and percentile latency targets | 2026-03-09

transcript:
[00:00] Alice Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we're going to dive into autoscaling and capacity planning for your use case - Maya, Samir, Lena, thanks for the time.
[00:12] Maya Patel: thanks Alice, yeah excited - we want to understand how Redwood can handle our daily 5000 concurrent users with the big midday spike, and especially the 2-3 minute bursts from the triage workflow.
[00:25] Diego Ramos: cool, can you quantify that burst? like qps or rps, and average tokens per request?
[00:32] Lena Wu: typical bursts are around 250 rps for 90-120 seconds, avg 120 tokens per response, sometimes up to 400 tokens for long summarizations.
[00:42] Samir Khan: and from infra we need to know reserved GPU sizing, how long nodes take to warm, and if we can avoid cold starts when hitting those bursts. We're on Azure, VPC peered to our account, want private deployment.
[00:55] Diego Ramos: ok that's helpful. quick primer: Redwood's autoscaler supports two orthogonal knobs - reserved capacity (you pre-commit GPUs) and burst capacity (we can either autoscale with cloud VMs or use a burst credit model in hosted). For private/VPC we usually recommend a hybrid: reserve baseline GPUs to hit steady-state plus a pre-warm window for expected bursts.
[01:15] Jordan Li: to add, the runtime has continuous batching, but batching increases latency at the low tail; so we tune target batch size and max wait to meet p95 SLOs. Also KV cache warm hits dramatically reduce per-token compute for long chats.
[01:30] Maya Patel: what about queueing? If a 250 rps burst comes in and we only have capacity for 100 rps, what's the model? do you backpressure or queue?
[01:41] Diego Ramos: good question. we use a hybrid queueing model. brief overview: requests enter front-door queue per route, small in-memory FIFO with timeouts. If capacity is saturated we have two policies: queue-and-wait up to a configured max latency, or immediate fallback to a cheaper model variant. For enterprise private we can also surface a rejection policy. The queue is per-instance-group and we dimension it to avoid head-of-line blocking across model shards.
[02:06] Lena Wu: you mentioned fallback to cheaper variant — how seamless is that? do embeddings vs small model and then rehydrate?
[02:13] Diego Ramos: seamless in the sense of routing; you can configure an automatic downgrade policy — e.g., route to a distilled 7B model when 30s wait time exceeded. It’s not rehydration of state; for stateful chat we try to preserve context by sending last KV snapshot and telling the app it was downgraded. Not ideal for generation fidelity, but it keeps latency bounded.
[02:31] Samir Khan: what about KV cache behavior under scale? if we have many short-lived requests, does cache become noisy and evict useful prefixes?
[02:40] Jordan Li: yes cache effectiveness depends on request locality. we expose a cache tier and eviction policy; for triage workflow where prefixes are similar it works well. we also support sticky routing so requests for the same session hit the same cache shard, reducing eviction. in private deployments, cache is memory backed on the serving nodes — you size RAM per GPU.
[03:02] Maya Patel: GPU warm time numbers? if you scale from 2 to 8 GPUs how long until they're useful?
[03:08] Diego Ramos: depends on infra; node provisioning often dominates (60-180s on clouds), container startup ~10-20s, model load quantized vs fp16 also matters — quantized LLs load faster. we recommend pre-pulling images and keeping a small pool of warm standby nodes. for on-prem you can keep a small hot pool to avoid cloud latency.
[03:26] Lena Wu: can you explain queueing math you use - is it like M/M/c or something custom?
[03:31] Diego Ramos: we approximate with M/M/c for capacity planning to estimate blocking probability, but production behavior uses trace-driven simulation considering variable token length and batching. the M/M/c is a starting point for deriving target number of servers to meet p95 latency. we also model batching as a tradeoff: large batch sizes improve throughput but increase wait.
[03:48] Maya Patel: example numbers? for our 250 rps burst with avg 120 tokens, what GPU count are we looking at?
[03:56] Diego Ramos: quick back-of-envelope — assume one GPU handles 12 TPS for that model/quantization profile (that's tokens-per-second, not requests). 250 req * 120 tokens = 30k tokens/sec. 30k / 12k per GPU = 2.5 GPUs so round up for headroom, maybe 4 GPUs baseline for the burst. But that hides batching gains; with smart batching throughput could double, so 2 GPUs might suffice with higher tail latency. Hence recommend reserving 2-3 baseline and allow 2-4 burst nodes.
[04:25] Samir Khan: how do you recommend setting target utilization? we don't want GPUs at 95% in prod.
[04:30] Jordan Li: typical target utilization 65-75% for latency-sensitive workloads; you can push higher for batchy inference. we also provide an autoscaler with percentile-based triggers — e.g., scale up when p95 latency exceeds threshold for N minutes.
[04:45] Owen Park: what about cost control during bursts? we worry about runaway billing.
[04:49] Alice Carter: two levers: reserved capacity pricing for predictable baseline, and burst credits (a capped usage pool) for unexpected spikes. You can configure hard caps and alerting; we also support manual approval workflows for very large bursts.
[05:05] Maya Patel: for VPC/private, are burst nodes spun in customer VPC or do you fall back to Redwood hosted?
[05:11] Diego Ramos: in private deployment we can either autoscale within the customer's capacity (spin VMs in the VPC) or use Redwood-hosted burst pool if the customer permits cross-connect routing. For regulated customers we usually keep everything inside the VPC and recommend some reserved headroom.
[05:26] Lena Wu: talk about quantization tradeoffs — we are assessing 4-bit and int8. how does that change performance and latency predictability?
[05:34] Jordan Li: quantization reduces memory and often improves throughput, but can add CPU/GPU overhead for dequant/decode steps. 4-bit quantization for many transformer weights yields 1.5–2x throughput improvement at small quality loss; int8 sometimes even more stable. You need to re-run evals for your prompts. Also cold start model loading time decreases with smaller checkpoint sizes.
[05:56] Maya Patel: any recommended A/B strategy for rolling quantized models? we don't want regression in accuracy.
[06:00] Diego Ramos: yes use canary rollout — route 5-10% of traffic to quantized variant, run quality checks on eval prompts, and have automatic rollback on drift. Redwood Console can surface per-prompt regressions and signal rollbacks.
[06:15] Samir Khan: curious about KV cache persistence across node restarts in private deploy.
[06:19] Jordan Li: by default KV cache is in-memory per shard; for heavier durability you can snapshot lightweight checkpoints to a shared store (S3/GCS or on-prem equivalent). Snapshotting adds some latency on restart but helps reduce cold-start recompute.
[06:34] Lena Wu: how do you size that RAM? our models have 50MB per session KV on average times 10k concurrent sessions ... that's huge.
[06:42] Diego Ramos: yep you can either shard sessions across many cache nodes or use sticky routing with eviction thresholds. For 10k sessions at 50MB that's 500GB, so you'd need a dedicated cache tier or tune session retention/TTL. Alternatively we support on-disk LRU tiers but that impacts latency.
[07:00] Maya Patel: some practical workflows — for triage we can tolerate p95 up to 2s, p99 up to 5s. Does that change your recommendations?
[07:07] Diego Ramos: yes that SLO is fairly tight. keep utilization lower (60%) and pre-warm extra GPUs for top-of-hour bursts. Also reduce max batching time to keep p99 down. Consider quantized models for throughput, but validate quality at p99.
[07:21] Owen Park: can you explain pre-warm policies? how do you trigger pre-warms ahead of predicted bursts?
[07:26] Jordan Li: we support scheduled pre-warms (based on known patterns) and predictive pre-warm using simple ML on historical traces—spin nodes N minutes before predicted spike. Also health-check and run synthetic warm requests to populate KV cache. Predictive pre-warm is configurable and can be tuned with false-positive cost thresholds.
[07:46] Maya Patel: what's the synthetic request? do you replay actual user prompts?
[07:50] Diego Ramos: we typically use anonymized representative prompts that warm the KV and model kernels without hitting downstream systems. You can provide a corpus; we can also generate synthetic tokens that mimic length distribution.
[07:59] Lena Wu: on batching, how do you configure max wait and batch size?
[08:04] Jordan Li: paramters are max_batch_size and max_queue_wait_ms. For latency-sensitive routes we set max_queue_wait_ms low (10-30ms) and smaller max_batch_size; for throughput-heavy embed routes we allow larger waits and batch sizes. Redwood Optimize can recommend settings per workload.
[08:20] Samir Khan: network egress and VPC peering — if we do host burst in Redwood, egress could be an issue for us compliance wise.
[08:27] Alice Carter: understood, that's why many regulated customers require in-VPC bursting. For that we work with your network team and can support AWS PrivateLink, Azure Private Link, and dedicated interconnects. We also provide audit logs and KMS integrations.
[08:41] Maya Patel: about metrics - what signals should we monitor to know we're underprovisioned?
[08:47] Diego Ramos: key metrics: token-per-second utilization per GPU, average batch sizes, queue depth, p95/p99 latency, cache hit rate, and model load times. Redwood Console can emit alerts on each with suggested remediation.
[09:01] Owen Park: do you do autoscaling cooldowns? we want to avoid thrash during oscillating traffic.
[09:06] Jordan Li: yes cooldown windows on scale-up and scale-down, and smoothing based on moving averages. You can configure aggressive or conservative policies. For your use case with short bursts we suggest shorter scale-up fast path but longer scale-down (so nodes stay warm for a bit).
[09:22] Maya Patel: can we limit scale-down so reserved GPUs never drop below baseline?
[09:25] Alice Carter: absolutely, you set min_replicas/reserved_pool. Scale-down won't touch reserved GPUs.
[09:31] Lena Wu: what's the instrumentation overhead - do we need special agents in VPC?
[09:36] Diego Ramos: we provide lightweight metrics exporters and can integrate with Prometheus or push to your monitoring. For private we typically deploy an agent in the control plane to ship metrics. Overhead is small.
[09:47] Maya Patel: any examples of customers with similar workloads?
[09:50] Alice Carter: yes a healthcare triage customer uses reserved baseline + predictive pre-warm for shift changes and kept p95 under 1.5s while saving ~40% cost vs overprovisioning. We can share a sanitized case study.
[10:02] Samir Khan: ok let's talk about targeted experiments - how do we validate performance on our data?
[10:07] Diego Ramos: we propose a two step POC: 1) trace-driven benchmark in Redwood lab using your anonymized trace to simulate bursts, measure p50/p95/p99, throughput, and cache hit; 2) small private deploy with reserved baseline and 1x burst node for real-world validation.
[10:23] Maya Patel: what resources do you need from us for the bench?
[10:26] Diego Ramos: anonymized request logs with token counts, peak schedule, and a small corpus of representative prompts for warm requests. Also creds for a temporary VPC test if we do on-prem sim.
[10:38] Lena Wu: for the bench, can you model different quantization levels so we can compare latency-quality-cost?
[10:43] Jordan Li: yes we'll run fp16 baseline, 8-bit, and 4-bit variants and produce a perf/quality matrix.
[10:50] Owen Park: timeline?
[10:52] Alice Carter: we can spin up a bench within 3 business days once we have traces. Diego will run 1-hour stress tests and share results within 5 days.
[11:00] Maya Patel: fine, let's do it. a couple nitpicks: we need SOC2 and data residency proof for any hosted fallback.
[11:07] Alice Carter: we'll attach SOC2 docs and outline residency options in the VPC doc.
[11:12] Samir Khan: last question: how do you handle many small concurrent sessions that each do short inference? we worry small requests will lead to poor batching and inefficient GPU use.
[11:20] Diego Ramos: for that we recommend mixing strategies: route tiny inference to CPU-backed embed services when applicable, or aggregate low-priority routes with larger max wait. You can also use a microservice pattern where prefiltering aggregates similar prompts server-side.
[11:36] Lena Wu: got it. anything else?
[11:38] Alice Carter: quick recap of next steps — Diego will run benchmark, I'll send the VPC doc and pricing, Maya to share traces. Owen to coordinate follow-up meeting.
[11:46] Owen Park: I'll create calendar invite for next Tuesday.
[11:48] Maya Patel: thank you all.
[11:50] Alice Carter: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with notes.
[11:55] [call ends]

Notes: transcription has occasional mislabels and truncated words, some technical terms may be slightly off (e.g., KV cache spelled out as K-V or KC). Links referenced: "VPC/private deployment architecture doc" (will be shared), "benchmarks spreadsheet" (to be created).
